trial_name: TRAIN — Restrictive vs Liberal Transfusion Strategy in Patients With Acute Brain Injury (2024)
citation: Taccone FS, Rynkowski Bittencourt C, Møller K, et al; TRAIN Study Group. Restrictive vs Liberal Transfusion Strategy in Patients With Acute Brain Injury: The TRAIN Randomized Clinical Trial. JAMA. 2024;332(19):1623-1633
one_liner: In anaemic ICU patients with acute brain injury, a liberal transfusion threshold (Hb <9 g/dL) reduced unfavourable 180-day neurological outcome compared with a restrictive threshold (Hb <7 g/dL) (62.6% vs 72.6%; aRR 0.86; P=0.002).

pico.population: Adults (18-80 years) with acute brain injury (TBI, SAH, ICH), GCS ≤13, Hb ≤9 g/dL, within 10 days of injury, expected ICU stay ≥72h and survival ≥24h
pico.intervention: Liberal transfusion strategy: transfuse RBCs if Hb <9 g/dL, target Hb ≥9 g/dL for up to 28 days or ICU discharge/death
pico.comparison: Restrictive transfusion strategy: transfuse RBCs if Hb <7 g/dL, target Hb ≥7 g/dL

background.existing_knowledge: Anaemia is common in neuro-ICU; general ICU evidence supports restrictive triggers (~7-8 g/dL), but neurocritical care patients were under-represented in foundational trials, and clinicians worry about secondary cerebral ischaemia.
background.knowledge_gap: Optimal transfusion thresholds for acute brain injury patients were uncertain due to lack of high-quality neuro-specific RCTs.
background.hypothesis: A liberal transfusion threshold (Hb <9 g/dL) would improve 180-day neurological outcome compared with a restrictive threshold (Hb <7 g/dL).

methods.design: Pragmatic, international, multicentre, randomised, open-label, parallel-group superiority trial with blinded assessment of 180-day functional outcome; 1:1 allocation; stratified by centre, acute brain injury type, and GCS (3-5, 6-9, 10-13) with variable block sizes (4,6,8). Primary analysis used modified intention-to-treat (excluding post-randomisation consent withdrawals) with adjusted risk ratios.
methods.setting: 72 ICUs across 22 countries; academic 57/72 (79.2%), non-academic 15/72 (20.8%); participants from high-income and low-/middle-income countries (low-/middle-income 229/827 [27.7%]).

inclusion: ICU physician anticipated ICU stay ≥72 hours and survival ≥24 hours
exclusion: Other acute neurological diagnoses (post-anoxic coma, ischaemic stroke, status epilepticus without underlying brain injury, CNS infections)
Active/uncontrolled bleeding or imminent surgery requiring transfusion
GCS 3 with bilaterally fixed dilated pupils
Clinical requirement to correct anaemia with target Hb >9 g/dL
Limitation of life-sustaining treatment at enrolment
History of alloimmunisation limiting RBC availability

methods.intervention: Liberal transfusion strategy: transfuse RBCs whenever Hb <9 g/dL, aiming to maintain Hb ≥9 g/dL. Strategy applied for up to 28 days after randomisation, or until ICU discharge/death. RBC product type and transfusion delivery followed local standards; co-interventions at clinician discretion.
methods.comparison: Restrictive transfusion strategy: transfuse RBCs whenever Hb <7 g/dL, aiming to maintain Hb ≥7 g/dL. Same exposure window. Permitted transfusion outside thresholds for clear clinical indications (e.g., uncontrolled bleeding) at clinician discretion.
methods.blinding: Treating teams not blinded; 180-day neurological outcome assessment performed by trained assessors blinded to group assignment.
methods.sample_size_power: 794 patients required to detect 11% absolute reduction in unfavourable neurological outcome (from 50% to 39%) with 85% power at two-sided 5% significance level; ultimately randomised 850 patients. A single interim analysis after 300 patients did not lead to early stopping.
secondary_outcomes: GOS-E ordinal shift analysis at 180 days
Composite death or any organ failure at 28 days
Acute respiratory distress syndrome (serious adverse event)
methods.follow_up: 180 days for primary outcome; key secondary outcomes and adverse events assessed to day 28 (or ICU/hospital discharge).

headline_bullets: Liberal strategy reduced unfavourable 180-day neurological outcome (62.6% vs 72.6%; aRR 0.86, 95% CI 0.79-0.94, P=0.002).
Substantial protocol separation: 86.9% vs 40.2% transfused; median 2 vs 0 RBC units.
Cerebral ischaemia less frequent with liberal strategy (8.8% vs 13.5%; RR 0.65, 95% CI 0.44-0.97).
No significant subgroup interactions; consistent benefit across TBI, SAH, ICH.

outcomes_table.note: Primary outcome; modified intention-to-treat; adjusted analysis

outcomes_table.outcome: GOS-E ordinal shift analysis at 180 days
outcomes_table.note: Higher odds of better functional outcome with liberal strategy

outcomes_table.outcome: Composite death or any organ failure at 28 days

outcomes_table.note: Direction favours liberal strategy; CI crosses 0
Direction favours liberal strategy; CI crosses 0

safety: Acute respiratory distress syndrome (SAE): 7.3% vs 8.5% (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.54-1.36)
Transfusion-related acute lung injury: 0% vs 0.5% (RR 0.21, 95% CI 0.01-4.31)
No clear increase in major transfusion-related complications with liberal strategy.

domains.notes: Centralised computer randomisation with stratification (centre, diagnosis, GCS) and variable block sizes; allocation concealment supported.

Open-label transfusion strategy; treating teams unblinded, permitting co-intervention bias; primary outcome assessment blinded, reducing detection bias for primary endpoint but not for clinician-diagnosed adverse events like cerebral ischaemia.

850 randomised; 30 withdrew consent post-randomisation (11 liberal, 19 restrictive) and excluded from modified ITT; primary outcome available for 806/820 (393/397 liberal, 413/423 restrictive); 14 missing primary outcomes.
Protocol violations low and similar (~5% in each arm); substantial separation in transfusion exposure (86.9% vs 40.2% transfused).
Groups broadly similar: median Hb 8.5 g/dL in both, median GCS 6 in both; TBI 58-61%, SAH 22-25%, ICH 17-18%.

internal_validity.verdict: Overall, internal validity is moderate-to-strong given central randomisation, strong protocol separation, and blinded primary outcome assessment; main threats are open-label care (performance/ascertainment bias) and exclusion of post-randomisation consent withdrawals.

domains.notes: Broad international enrolment (72 sites, 22 countries) supports generalisability; however, eligibility required Hb ≤9 g/dL and anticipated ICU stay ≥72h, selecting anaemic, sicker subset. Excluded other neurological diagnoses (post-anoxic coma, ischaemic stroke), active bleeding, limitations of life-sustaining treatment.

Findings apply to TBI, SAH, ICH in ICU; extrapolation to other neuro-ICU diagnoses uncertain. Implementation feasible where blood bank support exists, but increased transfusion utilisation may challenge resource-limited settings.

external_validity.verdict: External validity is good for adult ICU patients with moderate-to-severe acute brain injury and Hb ≤9 g/dL, but limited outside this anaemic neuro-ICU population and in settings where increased blood utilisation is not feasible.

strengths: Large, international, pragmatic neuro-ICU RCT addressing high-impact decision with equipoise.
Substantial protocol separation in transfusion exposure (86.9% vs 40.2% transfused; median 2 vs 0 units).
Patient-centred primary endpoint at 180 days with blinded assessment.
Consistent direction of effect across ordinal shift and sensitivity analyses.
limitations: Open-label design permits co-intervention bias and differential ascertainment of adverse events.
Modified ITT excluded 30 post-randomisation consent withdrawals; potential for bias if differential.
Heterogeneous brain injury syndromes limit syndrome-specific inference.
Eligibility restricted to anaemic patients with anticipated ICU stay ≥72h, limiting generalisability to less severe patients.

critical_appraisal.summary: TRAIN is a large, well-conducted RCT with strong protocol separation and blinded primary outcome assessment, demonstrating improved neurological outcomes with liberal transfusion in anaemic acute brain injury patients. Open-label design and post-randomisation exclusions introduce some risk of bias, but overall confidence in the primary result is moderate-to-high.
strengths: Large international sample with broad inclusion
weaknesses: Open-label care may influence co-interventions and adverse event ascertainment

sections.authors_conclusion: In anaemic ICU patients with acute brain injury, a liberal transfusion strategy (Hb <9 g/dL) improved 180-day neurological outcome compared with a restrictive strategy (Hb <7 g/dL), with a lower rate of cerebral ischaemia and no clear increase in major transfusion-related complications.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: A liberal transfusion threshold (Hb <9 g/dL) should be considered for anaemic ICU patients with acute brain injury to improve long-term neurological outcomes, challenging routine restrictive thresholds in neurocritical care.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: Adult ICU patients with moderate-to-severe acute brain injury (TBI, SAH, ICH) and Hb ≤9 g/dL, without active bleeding or imminent surgery requiring transfusion.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not mean all neuro-ICU patients should receive liberal transfusions; benefit was shown in anaemic patients, and open-label design may have influenced outcomes. Also does not imply liberal transfusion reduces mortality.
implementation_caveats: Increased blood product utilisation (86.9% vs 40.2% transfused) requires assessment of local blood availability and stewardship.
Open-label nature means co-interventions may have contributed; consider integrating with other neuro-specific RCTs like HEMOTION.
Benefit was in neurological outcome, not mortality; shared decision-making with families about goals of care is important.

controversies.notes: The trial protocol was amended during the trial, with revised sample size assumptions; while prespecified safeguards were in place, optimistic effect-size assumptions in the final power calculation raise concerns about potential overestimation of benefit.

Unblinded transfusion strategy could influence clinician behaviour (neuro-monitoring, imaging, treatment limitation decisions), potentially contributing to between-group differences beyond the transfusion itself; blinded 180-day outcome assessment reduces but does not eliminate this threat.
Dichotomising GOS-E at 1-5 vs 6-8 may discard information; however, ordinal shift analysis and sensitivity analysis using GOS-E 1-4 remained supportive, strengthening robustness.

In the HEMOTION trial (TBI-specific), a more liberal threshold (Hb <10 g/dL) did not significantly reduce unfavourable 6-month outcome vs restrictive (Hb <7 g/dL), highlighting residual uncertainty about effect magnitude and potential heterogeneity across injury types and thresholds.

Prior systematic reviews emphasised low certainty and heterogeneity in brain-injury transfusion literature; TRAIN provides high-quality evidence that will update meta-analyses and guidelines, but integration with other large RCTs is needed to assess net benefit and subgroup effects.

context_related_trials.relation: Large TBI-specific RCT comparing liberal (Hb <10 g/dL) vs restrictive (Hb <7 g/dL); did not show significant reduction in unfavourable 6-month outcome, contrasting with TRAIN's positive result and suggesting potential heterogeneity or threshold-dependent effects.

unresolved_questions: Optimal Hb threshold for different brain injury subtypes (TBI vs SAH vs ICH) remains uncertain.
Whether a threshold of 9 g/dL is superior to 10 g/dL or 8 g/dL is unknown.
Role of liberal transfusion in non-anaemic or less severe brain injury patients is unclear.
Long-term functional outcomes beyond 180 days and cost-effectiveness need further study.
Interaction with other neuroprotective strategies and co-interventions requires exploration.

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: In anaemic acute brain injury patients, a liberal transfusion strategy (Hb <9 g/dL) improves 180-day neurological outcome compared with restrictive (Hb <7 g/dL), challenging routine restrictive thresholds in neurocritical care.
